newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Schindler starts 1997 on track.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Schindler starts 1997 on track.

text.p: Schindler Holding AG, one of the world's leading makers of escalators and elevators, on Thursday said business had started well in 1997 and it was confident of achieving its profit target for the year.

The world's leading escalator maker and second-largest elevator producer expects profits this year to jump to 160 million Swiss francs ($111.3 million), before restructuring costs of 25 million, from 1996's 88.5 million.
"We have no doubt at the moment that we will achieve this goal for 1997," chief financial officer Alfred Spoerri said.
Schindler, which has suffered from a slump in worldwide prices due to recession and gruelling price wars, said its outlook was based partly on a line of new products that are being launched.
"The year 1997 has started well and new orders are going as planned," Peter Szbinden, president of the main elevator and escalator business, told Schindler's annual news conference.
New products include a low price model 001 in Italy, a new 9300 escalator line and a breakthrough in elevator technology due to be presented in Munich on April 15.
"I expect very good market acceptance for these products," Szbinden said.
Schindler said anti-cartel laws would be a major barrier to any potential acquisition of the elevator business of Germany's Thyssen AG.
It expects continued growth in the Asian elevator and escalator market and a slight rebound in North America and Latin America.
While there are few signs of an improvement in demand or prices in most European markets, Schindler hopes new products this spring will boost sales.

Spoerri said Schindler's operating margin in 1996, before extraordinary costs for restructuring, was 3.4 percent, up from 2.8 percent in 1995 but still only about one-third of the level at the world's largest elevator maker, Otis, part of U.S. group United Technologies Corp.
"We still have to catch up quite a bit to the best of the class (Otis)," Spoerri said.

Asked whether Schindler would be interested in Thyssen's elevator unit if it were to come on the market, chairman Alfred Schindler told reporters that prices were very high for that kind of business at the moment.
One issue was whether a high purchase price would detract from the company's interest in pursuing internal growth.
"In principle there is no reason not to pursue it (if the Thyssen business came on the market) but in many cases we would simply not be permitted to by cartel law," Schindler said.

"Cartel laws, especially in the United States, are very tough," he said, responding to a question about what would happen if Thyssen decided to spin off its elevator business as part of cooperation with Krupp KFHG.F AG.

Schindler said there was only limited room for accommodating anti-cartel authorities with spin-offs or other portfolio adjustments and the price for any such acquisition would be another major factor.
"The price for medium to large companies is generally at least equivalent to annual sales," he said, adding: "Then you would also be in direct competition with your internal growth."

Schindler said earlier in the news conference that the group needed to grow to keep up with a competitive world market but would concentrate on internal growth because only a few independent companies remained to be bought after more than a decade of consolidation in the industry.
Other factors to consider would be whether an acquisition was located in a country with higher or lower growth and whether its product line was complementary, he said.
